terms.gloss: advantage, a good point; the good one gets from a thing
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.335: commoda pācis … itemque incommoda contrāriōrum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “advantage, profit (very freq. in all periods)”. A thing’s advantages and drawbacks are its commoda et incommoda; for a drawback alone see problem (incommodum). Also convenience: cum erit tuum commodum, when it suits you (Cic. Att. 12.28.3, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: usefulness, advantage; in the plural, the benefits of a thing
evidence: Cic. Lael. 32: sīc et ūtilitātēs ex amīcitiā maximae capientur
terms.comment: What a thing is good for; in Cicero’s ethics the useful, as against the honourable.

terms.gloss: it is an advantage, it does good
terms.grammar: verb: third person of prōsum, with the dative of the person; what helps is the subject (a noun or an infinitive)
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.64: multum prōdest ea, quae metuuntur, ipsa contemnere
Traupman 92: to be of advantage, prōsum
terms.comment: “The advantage of X is …” is often turned with the verb: quid prōdest?, what is the advantage? See benefit.

terms.gloss: count as gain, consider a plus
evidence: Ter. Ph. 2.1.16: omne id dēputāre esse in lucrō (Lewis & Short s.v. lucrum)
Traupman 105: consider it a plus, id dēputā esse in lucrō
terms.comment: “To reckon it among the profits”: whatever turns out better than feared is clear gain.

phrases.latin: quī ūtilitātem dēfendet, ēnumerābit commoda pācis, opum, potentiae, vectīgālium … itemque incommoda contrāriōrum
phrases.english: whoever argues for advantage will list the advantages of peace, wealth, power and revenue … and likewise the disadvantages of their opposites

phrases.latin: multum prōdest ea, quae metuuntur, ipsa contemnere
phrases.english: there is great advantage in despising the very things that are feared

phrases.latin: omne id dēputāre esse in lucrō
phrases.english: to count all that as gain

sources: Lewis & Short: commodum · Lewis & Short: utilitas · Lewis & Short: prosum
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 92.
Cicero, De oratore 2, Tusculans 1 and 4 and Laelius, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
